title: The Nose That Bleeds Every Week
subtitle: A woman with a lifetime of nosebleeds, from the family history to the organs you cannot see
description: Recognizing the pattern, examining and counting the Curacao criteria, screening for the arteriovenous malformations that kill, controlling an acute bleed without making the next one worse, the treatment ladder for the nose, and what to do when it will not stop.

steps.title: Step 1/6: The Pattern
steps.scenario:
A 42-year-old woman is referred for nosebleeds.

    Frequency       three or four a week
    Duration        since her teens, worse over the last five years
    Trigger         none; most start at rest or wake her at night
    Side            either, often both
    Cautery         four times at different clinics, each helped for weeks
    Anticoagulant   none
    Trauma          none
    Hypertension    none

She is tired and short of breath climbing stairs. Hemoglobin 9.1 g/dL, ferritin 6 ng/mL.

Her father and her older brother both have frequent nosebleeds.
steps.question: Which features make this more than ordinary epistaxis?

options.text: (A) The iron deficiency alone; the bleeding pattern itself is common
(B) Spontaneous, recurrent bleeding since adolescence, with two affected first-degree relatives and iron-deficiency anemia
(C) Nothing; repeated cautery failure means the technique was inadequate
(D) The bilateral bleeding, which always means a coagulopathy

steps.feedback:
Correct answer: B

Ordinary epistaxis is anterior, provoked, occasional, and it stops. Hers is none of those. Four features together change the question from where is it bleeding to why does she bleed.
• Spontaneous and recurrent, without trauma, dry air or anticoagulation.
• Starting in adolescence and worsening with age, which is the natural history of hereditary hemorrhagic telangiectasia: nosebleeds usually begin around age 12, and the number and size of telangiectasias increase over decades.
• Two affected first-degree relatives. HHT is autosomal dominant, so a parent and a sibling with the same symptom is a pedigree, not a coincidence.
• Iron-deficiency anemia, which tells you how much blood she is actually losing. A hemoglobin of 9.1 with a ferritin of 6 is chronic loss, not the four episodes she remembers best.

Cautery that works for a few weeks and then fails is also characteristic: the lesions are multiple and they keep forming, so treating one spot does not treat the disease.

Why the others fail:
(A) The anemia matters, but on its own it says only that she is losing blood. It is the combination with the pattern and the family history that points to a diagnosis.
(C) Four operators is unlikely to be four failures of technique. Recurrence after adequate cautery is a feature of the disease.
(D) Bilateral bleeding does not mean coagulopathy. Her platelet count and clotting screen will be normal; HHT is a disease of vessel wall structure, not of clotting.

Keypoint: spontaneous recurrent epistaxis since adolescence, a family history, and iron deficiency is HHT until you have looked for telangiectasias.

Reference: Faughnan ME, Mager JJ, Hetts SW, et al. Second International Guidelines for the Diagnosis and Management of Hereditary Hemorrhagic Telangiectasia. Ann Intern Med. 2020;173(12):989-1001. doi:10.7326/M20-1443.

steps.title: Step 2/6: The Examination and the Count
steps.scenario:
You examine her.

    Lips              three small red spots on the vermilion, blanching
    Tongue            two on the dorsum
    Fingertips        two on the right hand
    Nasal endoscopy   multiple telangiectasias on both sides of the septum and the inferior turbinates

History:

    Epistaxis         spontaneous, recurrent, since her teens
    Family            father and brother with the same nosebleeds; never formally diagnosed
    Visceral lesions  none known; never investigated
steps.media: Load image: Nasal endoscopy from this patient, de-identified, unannotated: telangiectasias on the septum and inferior turbinate. Caption: 'Nasal endoscopy.'
steps.question: How many Curacao criteria does she meet, and what is her diagnosis?

options.text: (A) Three: definite HHT
(B) Two: possible HHT, because the relatives were never diagnosed
(C) Three: possible HHT, because no visceral lesion has been found
(D) Four: definite HHT

steps.feedback:
Correct answer: A

Where to look. The telangiectasias of HHT have characteristic sites, and knowing them turns a two-minute examination into a diagnosis: the lips, especially the vermilion border; the tongue; the buccal and palatal mucosa; the fingertips and nail beds; and the nasal mucosa on endoscopy, usually the septum and anterior turbinates. Each lesion is 1 to 3 mm, red to purple, flat, and blanches. They are not spider angiomas, which fill from a central arteriole outward. Photograph them; the number grows over the years.

The Curacao criteria are four:
1. Spontaneous, recurrent epistaxis.
2. Multiple telangiectasias at characteristic sites: lips, oral cavity, fingers, nose.
3. Visceral lesions: pulmonary, cerebral, hepatic, spinal or gastrointestinal AVMs or telangiectasias.
4. A first-degree relative with HHT.

Three or more: definite. Two: possible. Fewer: unlikely.

She has epistaxis, telangiectasias at three sites, and a first-degree relative. Three, and three is definite. A relative does not need a laboratory diagnosis to count: a father and brother with the same pattern of spontaneous recurrent epistaxis satisfy the criterion clinically. What she does not have is a visceral lesion, and that is because nobody has looked. The criteria do not require one.

Why the others fail:
(B) The relatives count. The fourth criterion is a first-degree relative with HHT by these criteria, and two relatives with lifelong spontaneous epistaxis meet it.
(C) Visceral involvement is one of the four criteria, not a requirement for the diagnosis. Three of any four make it definite.
(D) She has no documented visceral lesion, so that criterion is not met yet. Count what you have.

Keypoint: lips, tongue, mouth, fingertips, nose; epistaxis, telangiectasias, visceral lesion, relative; three of four is definite HHT, and a visceral lesion is not required.

Reference: Shovlin CL, Guttmacher AE, Buscarini E, et al. Diagnostic criteria for hereditary hemorrhagic telangiectasia (Rendu-Osler-Weber syndrome). Am J Med Genet. 2000;91(1):66-67. Faughnan ME, Mager JJ, Hetts SW, et al. Ann Intern Med. 2020;173(12):989-1001.

steps.title: Step 3/6: The Organs You Cannot See
steps.scenario:
Definite HHT. She has never been screened for anything and is well apart from the nosebleeds and the anemia: no headaches, no seizures, no breathlessness at rest, no hemoptysis.

She has two children, 14 and 11, both well.
steps.question: What screening does she need, and which comes first?

options.text: (A) None; she has no symptoms of visceral involvement
(B) Contrast (agitated saline) transthoracic echocardiography for pulmonary AVM, and MRI of the brain with contrast for cerebral AVM; hepatic imaging if there are symptoms or signs
(C) Chest radiograph and routine liver function tests
(D) CT of the chest, head and abdomen in one sitting

steps.feedback:
Correct answer: B

The nosebleeds are what she came for. The arteriovenous malformations are what can kill her, and they are silent until they are not.

Pulmonary AVM, first and most important.
• Screen with contrast transthoracic echocardiography, the agitated saline bubble study: bubbles appearing in the left heart after three or more cycles indicate a right-to-left shunt.
• A positive study is followed by CT of the chest to size and map the lesions, and large ones are treated by transcatheter embolization.
• The reason for urgency is not hypoxia. It is that blood bypassing the pulmonary capillary filter carries clots and bacteria straight to the brain: ischemic stroke and brain abscess, in young and otherwise healthy people.
• Anyone with HHT also needs antibiotic prophylaxis before dental and other procedures, and meticulous avoidance of air in intravenous lines, because a filter that should be there is not.

Cerebral AVM.
• MRI of the brain with contrast, once in adults, and in children at diagnosis.
• Lesions found are discussed with a neurovascular team; not all are treated.

The family. HHT is autosomal dominant, so each child has a 50 percent chance. Test her first, because she certainly carries the variant (ENG, ACVRL1, or SMAD4); once it is found, testing the children is a single targeted test. And the children are screened for pulmonary AVM whether or not they have symptoms, because a child with no nosebleeds can still have the shunt.

Hepatic involvement is common but usually asymptomatic; the guidelines do not recommend routine screening in the absence of symptoms or abnormal liver tests, and Doppler ultrasound is the first test when it is indicated. Gastrointestinal telangiectasias are investigated when the anemia is out of proportion to the epistaxis.

Why the others fail:
(A) Absence of symptoms is the reason to screen. A pulmonary AVM large enough to cause a stroke often causes nothing beforehand.
(C) A chest radiograph misses most pulmonary AVMs and liver function tests miss most hepatic involvement. Neither is a screening test for this.
(D) Whole-body CT is not the pathway: the bubble study comes before chest CT, brain screening is by MRI not CT, and routine abdominal imaging is not recommended without an indication.

Keypoint: bubble echo for the lungs, contrast MRI for the brain; test her before the children, then screen the children; and everyone with HHT gets antibiotic prophylaxis and an air filter on the drip.

Reference: Faughnan ME, Mager JJ, Hetts SW, et al. Second International Guidelines for the Diagnosis and Management of Hereditary Hemorrhagic Telangiectasia. Ann Intern Med. 2020;173(12):989-1001. doi:10.7326/M20-1443.

steps.title: Step 4/6: In the Emergency Department
steps.scenario:
Three weeks later she is in the emergency department at 2 a.m.

    Bleeding      left side, brisk, 40 minutes, not stopping with pressure
    BP            118/74, pulse 96
    Hemoglobin    8.6 g/dL
    Endoscopy     oozing from several telangiectasias on the anterior septum; the mucosa around them is thin and friable

The emergency physician has a non-absorbable pack ready and asks whether to use it.
steps.question: How do you control this bleed?

options.text: (A) Tight bilateral non-absorbable packing for 72 hours
(B) Bipolar cautery of both sides of the septum under local anesthesia
(C) Head up, topical vasoconstrictor and tranexamic acid, gentle absorbable or lubricated packing if needed, and targeted bipolar or laser to the bleeding points only
(D) Emergency sphenopalatine artery ligation

steps.feedback:
Correct answer: C

An HHT nose is not an ordinary nose, and the emergency department's reflexes can make it worse. The mucosa is thin, the vessels are superficial, and every pack that goes in and every pack that comes out tears more of them.

What works, in order:
• Sit her up, pinch the soft part of the nose, ten minutes by the clock. Most HHT bleeds stop with that.
• Topical vasoconstrictor, oxymetazoline on a pledget, and topical or oral tranexamic acid.
• If packing is needed, use a dissolvable hemostatic material or a lubricated, low-pressure pack, and remove it early. Never pack tightly, never pack for days.
• If a bleeding point can be seen, treat that point: bipolar at low power, or KTP or diode laser, to the telangiectasia and nothing around it.

What to avoid, and why:
• Non-absorbable packing tears the mucosa on removal and starts the next bleed; it also carries the risk of toxic shock. The nosebleed guideline says packing is a bridge, not a treatment, and in HHT the bridge is more expensive than usual.
• Cautery of both sides of the septum in one sitting, or cautery of wide areas, leads to perforation. A septal perforation in HHT is permanent and bleeds more than the septum did.
• Silver nitrate on friable HHT mucosa is imprecise and spreads.

Why the others fail:
(A) Tight packing for three days will stop this bleed and cause the next one, and in the meantime she cannot breathe through her nose and is at risk of toxic shock. In HHT the aim is to avoid packing, not to prolong it.
(B) Bilateral septal cautery at the same sitting is the classic way to make a septal perforation. One side, and only the bleeding points.
(D) Sphenopalatine artery ligation is an operation for a single arterial bleeding point in ordinary posterior epistaxis. Her bleeding is from many superficial vessels supplied by collaterals; ligating one artery does not stop them for long, and it takes away an embolization route.

Keypoint: pressure, vasoconstrictor, tranexamic acid, gentle packing only if you must and out early; cautery to the bleeding point, never to the whole septum, never both sides.

Reference: Faughnan ME, Mager JJ, Hetts SW, et al. Ann Intern Med. 2020;173(12):989-1001. Tunkel DE, Anne S, Payne SC, et al. Clinical practice guideline: nosebleed (epistaxis). Otolaryngol Head Neck Surg. 2020;162(1_suppl):S1-S38. doi:10.1177/0194599819890327.

steps.title: Step 5/6: Controlling It Long Term
steps.scenario:
The bleed is controlled. Now the longer question.

    Bleeds        three or four a week, 10 to 20 minutes each
    Effect        avoids meetings and travel, wakes at night
    Hemoglobin    8.6 g/dL, ferritin 6 ng/mL
    Previous      four cauteries, each effective for weeks

She asks what can actually be done.
steps.question: Where do you start?

options.text: (A) Humidification and topical moisturizers, oral tranexamic acid, and iron replacement; ablation with KTP or diode laser for lesions that keep bleeding
(B) Silver nitrate cautery to every visible telangiectasia today
(C) Septodermoplasty now, since cautery has already failed four times
(D) Bilateral sphenopalatine artery ligation

steps.feedback:
Correct answer: A

HHT epistaxis is managed in a ladder, and the rungs are climbed only as far as necessary. Start at the bottom, always, because the treatments higher up are irreversible or systemic.

First rung, and it is not optional:
• Humidification, saline gel and moisturizers, kept up daily. A dry crust tearing off a telangiectasia is how many bleeds start.
• Avoid nose-picking, forceful blowing, and NSAIDs where possible.
• Iron replacement, oral or intravenous, and treat the anemia as a condition in its own right. Her ferritin of 6 needs replacing whatever happens to the bleeding.

Second rung:
• Oral tranexamic acid reduces bleeding in HHT and is recommended for patients whose epistaxis is not controlled by moisturizing.
• Topical tranexamic acid, bevacizumab and estriol were tested against saline in a randomized trial and none beat placebo, so the topical route is not the answer.

Third rung:
• Ablation of individual lesions: KTP or diode laser, or bipolar at low power. The laser wavelengths are absorbed by hemoglobin, which lets you close a vessel while sparing the mucosa around it. Repeated ablation is expected; it controls, it does not cure.

Why the others fail:
(B) Cauterizing every lesion damages the mucosa between them, and new lesions form anyway. Targeted ablation of the ones that bleed is the approach, not a scorched septum.
(C) Septodermoplasty is a later rung, for bleeding refractory to ablation and medical therapy. Four office cauteries is not the same as failed systematic treatment.
(D) Sphenopalatine artery ligation is an operation for a single arterial bleeding point in ordinary posterior epistaxis. HHT bleeding is from hundreds of fragile superficial vessels, and ligating the supply does not stop them for long.

Keypoint: moisturize, replace the iron, add tranexamic acid, ablate selectively with KTP or diode; do not scorch the septum and do not ligate.

Reference: Faughnan ME, Mager JJ, Hetts SW, et al. Ann Intern Med. 2020;173(12):989-1001. Whitehead KJ, Sautter NB, McWilliams JP, et al. Effect of topical intranasal therapy on epistaxis frequency in patients with hereditary hemorrhagic telangiectasia: a randomized clinical trial. JAMA. 2016;316(9):943-951.

steps.title: Step 6/6: When It Will Not Stop
steps.scenario:
Eighteen months later. She has used moisturizers daily, taken tranexamic acid, and had three sessions of KTP ablation.

    Bleeds        still four or five a week
    Transfusions  three units in the past six months
    Hemoglobin    8.4 g/dL despite intravenous iron
    Work          has stopped working

Pulmonary AVMs were found and embolized; brain MRI normal.
steps.question: What do you consider now?

options.text: (A) More frequent KTP sessions, every six weeks indefinitely
(B) Long-term nasal packing to keep the mucosa compressed
(C) External carotid artery ligation
(D) Systemic antiangiogenic therapy with bevacizumab, and surgical options such as septodermoplasty or nasal closure if that fails

steps.feedback:
Correct answer: D

She has climbed the ladder and is still bleeding, still transfusion-dependent, and no longer working. That is severe, refractory HHT epistaxis, and it is where systemic therapy enters.

Systemic antiangiogenic therapy.
• Bevacizumab, an anti-VEGF antibody given intravenously, reduces epistaxis severity and transfusion requirement in severe HHT. The Second International Guidelines recommend considering it for patients with severe bleeding or anemia not controlled by local therapy and iron.
• It is given in a center that knows the drug, with attention to hypertension, proteinuria and wound healing, and the effect wears off, so maintenance dosing is usual.
• Other systemic agents, including pazopanib and thalidomide, have been used in refractory disease and are options in specialized hands.

Surgery, when systemic therapy fails or cannot be given.
• Septodermoplasty: the fragile septal mucosa is removed and replaced with a split-thickness skin graft. It reduces bleeding, at the cost of crusting and smell, and telangiectasias eventually appear in the graft.
• Young's procedure: the nostrils are surgically closed. It is the most effective operation for refractory HHT epistaxis and the most radical, because she will breathe through her mouth permanently. It is reserved for the patient for whom the bleeding has become the whole of life, and hers is close to that.

And the anemia is treated in parallel, not afterward: intravenous iron at whatever interval she needs, and transfusion as required. Hemoglobin is the outcome the patient feels.

Why the others fail:
(A) Ablation every six weeks is what she is already failing, and repeated mucosal injury eventually causes perforation.
(B) Long-term packing damages the mucosa, does not stop new lesions, and adds the risks of infection and toxic shock. In HHT the goal is to avoid packing, not to prolong it.
(C) External carotid ligation removes the option of embolization later, is followed by recruitment of collateral supply, and has no role in a disease of diffuse superficial vessels.

Keypoint: refractory HHT epistaxis goes to systemic bevacizumab, then septodermoplasty or nasal closure; and the anemia is treated all the way through.

Reference: Faughnan ME, Mager JJ, Hetts SW, et al. Second International Guidelines for the Diagnosis and Management of Hereditary Hemorrhagic Telangiectasia. Ann Intern Med. 2020;173(12):989-1001. doi:10.7326/M20-1443.
